answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — actually Ursula K. Le Guin
answer.authorDates: 1929–2018 · American author of science fiction & fantasy
answer.sourceLine: This is a real, verified line — but it is not Hemingway’s. It comes from Ursula K. Le Guin’s 1969 novel The Left Hand of Darkness, Chapter 15, spoken during the crossing of the Gobrin Ice. The Ernest Hemingway credit only appears from around 2010 — nearly half a century after Hemingway’s death.

source.heading: The real source
source.excerpt: It is good to have an end to journey towards; but it is the journey that matters, in the end.
trail: 1969 — the origin. Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Left Hand of Darkness (Chapter 15) contains the line as originally published, per Quote Investigator.
1977 onward — correctly credited. The line was attributed to Le Guin in The Quotable Woman: 1800–1975 (1977) and later reference works, as documented by Quote Investigator.
c. 2010 — the Hemingway error. The earliest located Hemingway credit is a 2010 obituary — roughly 50 years after Hemingway’s 1961 death, per Quote Investigator.
Text-verified. The quotation database WIST records the line to The Left Hand of Darkness, Chapter 15 (1969).
source.excerptNote: The narrator reflects on the long, punishing trek across the Gobrin Glacier — the line is a meditation on the value of the journey itself, not a stand-alone aphorism. Note the original wording is “towards”; later reprints and quote sites often shorten it to “toward.”
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Ursula K. Le Guin / Ace Books (Penguin Random House)
source.rightsNote: The Left Hand of Darkness was first published in 1969 and remains under U.S. copyright; Le Guin died in 2018 and her work is controlled by her estate and publisher. This is a genuine literary quotation, not public-domain wisdom.

author.heading: About Ursula K. Le Guin
author.metaLine: 1929–2018 · American novelist of science fiction & fantasy
author.bio: Ursula K. Le Guin (1929–2018) was one of the most acclaimed American authors of speculative fiction, best known for the Earthsea series and the Hainish Cycle. The Left Hand of Darkness (1969), the source of this line, won both the Hugo and Nebula awards and is a landmark exploration of gender and journeying. Her prose is threaded with quietly aphoristic lines like this one, which is exactly why it travels so easily — often stripped of her name.

misattribution.heading: How Hemingway got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a genuine quotation — the misattribution is about who wrote it, not whether it’s real. The line is Le Guin’s; Hemingway is a later, spurious credit.

items.why: Hemingway is by far the most common name attached to this line online, yet he died in 1961 and the earliest located Hemingway credit is a 2010 obituary — a gap of nearly 50 years. There is no evidence he ever said or wrote it, per Quote Investigator.
Le Guin’s original reads “an end to journey towards”; many reprints and quote sites shorten it to “toward,” a change traced at least to a 1990 anthology by Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are really Ursula K. Le Guin’s, written in The Left Hand of Darkness (1969, Ch. 15) — not Ernest Hemingway’s, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Within the novel the line lands at the end of a brutal months-long trek across a glacier — a physical journey that has become the emotional heart of the story. Pulled out of the book and pinned on Hemingway, it reads like generic inspirational wisdom; in context it is the hard-won reflection of a character who has nearly died getting somewhere.
Its journey-over-destination theme is ancient, and Quote Investigator notes an echo in a 1920 line by theologian Lynn H. Hough — but the specific, memorable wording is Le Guin’s own.
context.pull: It is the journey that matters, in the end.
